fetched_contents.text: Self-employment experience effects on well-being: A longitudinal study Abstract The notion that self-employed individuals are more satisfied with their jobs than wage-employees has found broad empirical support. Previous research exploring the well-being effects of self-employment typically relies on direct cross-sectional comparisons between wage-employees and self-employed or on longitudinal investigations of transitions in or out of self-employment. In this study, the authors use individuals’ employment status histories in British longitudinal data to examine how accumulated self-employment experience affects job satisfaction, satisfaction with leisure and satisfaction with income. The study finds that those with past work experience only as self-employed report higher levels of job satisfaction than those with experience only as wage-employees. However, individuals with mixed work experience profiles are the most satisfied. This suggests a non-monotonic relationship between self-employment and job satisfaction. Patterns of self-employment experience and other satisfaction domains, such as satisfaction with income or leisure, are more nuanced, differing across gender lines. Introduction The number of individuals who enter self-employment in the United Kingdom has steadily risen since 2001, reaching almost 15% of all civilian employment (Yuen et al., 2018). This raises a question: why do people choose to follow a riskier career in self-employment over a more secure one in wage-employment? There is by now a large body of literature exploring the motives, conditions and characteristics that influence individuals’ decisions to become entrepreneurs. Empirical work looks, for example, at risk-seeking and opportunity (Ajayi-Obe and Parker, 2005; Brachert et al., 2019), work–life balance (König and Cesinger, 2015; Munkejord, 2017), genetic proclivity (Nicolaou et al., 2008) and personality (Patel and Thatcher, 2014) as the main drivers of self-employment. Similarly, individuals cite greater autonomy, flexibility and independence as the main reasons for individuals deciding to start up a business (Benz and Frey, 2008a; Hundley, 2001; Murgia and Pulignano, 2021; Shir et al., 2019). Others view self-employment as an opportunity to pursue a meaningful work experience (Frey et al., 2004; McMullen and Dimov, 2013; Nikolaev et al., 2020; Shepherd and Patzelt, 2017). Some individuals will also turn to self-employment out of necessity (Block and Koellinger, 2009; Koch et al., 2021). Studies also underline job satisfaction and well-being as the main motivating reasons for self-employment transitions (Douglas and Shepherd, 2002; Guerra and Patuelli, 2016). More recently, Nikolova (2019) highlights the beneficial effects on health for both necessity and opportunity motivated transitions. Prior research typically finds that the self-employed report higher levels of job satisfaction compared to wage-employees (Abreu et al., 2019; Georgellis et al., 2007; Román et al., 2013). Many self-employed attribute their higher job satisfaction to both financial and nonfinancial benefits (Benz and Frey, 2004; Burke et al., 2002; Lofstrom et al., 2014). Quadrini (2000) finds that switching from wage-employment to self-employment, more often than not, leads to increased social standing. Additionally, self-employed individuals enjoy higher living standards compared to wage-employees (Carter, 2011). They also report high income satisfaction, despite income-stream uncertainty and volatility (Parker et al., 2005). Nevertheless, Guerra and Patuelli (2016) argue that those who switch from wage-employment to self-employment do so as a response to dissatisfaction with nonpecuniary benefits, such as job flexibility and independence. There are also unwelcome, nonfinancial aspects of business ownership. Long work hours and the personal energy demands of managing a business increase stress and anxiety, which dampen job satisfaction following a self-employment transition (Bradley and Roberts, 2004; Jamal, 1997; Schonfeld and Mazzola, 2015). Recent evidence suggests that overtime, mental and physical stress are damaging entrepreneurs’ well-being (Mattes, 2016; Patel et al., 2019). Furthermore, it is sometimes difficult for the self-employed to disengage from work (Kirkwood and Tootell, 2008; Lott, 2020). Studies show that while transitions from wage-employment to self-employment result in higher job satisfaction, they impact negatively leisure satisfaction (Binder and Coad, 2016; van der Zwan et al., 2018). Most previous empirical work relies on cross-sectional samples that examine how self-employment impacts well-being at a single point in time (Dimov, 2011; Stephan, 2018). A growing number of longitudinal studies have explored well-being following self-employment transitions. Typically, longitudinal analyses document a transitory job satisfaction boost from transitions to self-employment (Binder and Coad, 2016; Bradley and Roberts, 2004; Georgellis and Yusuf, 2016; Mattes, 2016; Stenard, 2019; van der Zwan et al., 2018). A drawback of such analyses is that they do not usually consider multiple transitions in and out of self-employment. This is despite evidence suggesting the self-employed follow more diverse employment patterns than wage-employees (Åstebro and Thompson, 2011; Lazear, 2005; Lechmann and Schnabel, 2014). Deviating from earlier empirical work, in this article we consider self-employment as part of a career path to examine how past self-employment experience influences well-being. fetched_contents.text: Well-being effects of self-employment: A spatial inquiry Executive summary The recognition that individuals choose to become entrepreneurs for a range of reasons over and above financial motives, and that they benefit from entrepreneurship in a number of non-financial ways, have led to the emergence of a young and rapidly growing strand of literature that investigates the link between entrepreneurship and well-being. Although the initial focus was limited to job satisfaction, more recent studies have investigated the link between entrepreneurship and a wider range of well-being measures and concluded that entrepreneurs may be prioritising job satisfaction to the detriment of other aspects of their well-being. One particular issue that this strand of literature is silent about is the potential importance of location for entrepreneurial well-being – a gap we aim to fill with this paper. The entrepreneurship literature is vast when it comes to discussing the importance of contextual determinants of entrepreneurship, highlighting factors such as the presence of social networks, labour market thickness, and transport links. If entrepreneurial activity varies in its nature and performance across space, then so might the outcomes of entrepreneurship, including well-being. The literature on well-being is similarly very vocal about the importance of spatial context, and one aspect that is commonly discussed is the urban/rural dimension. We argue that while an urban environment may provide the entrepreneur with the necessary market scale and scope to secure a successful business, it may also impose a number of negative externalities on the individual's well-being due to, for example, high living costs, congestion, commuting times, pollution, and crime. Such trade-offs suggest that a binary categorization of cities into an urban-rural dichotomy may lead to an incomplete analysis of the importance of location. Rather, we argue, places that rank between the urban and rural locations may provide a better climate for realizing both higher entrepreneurial well-being and entrepreneurial success. We also argue that, at the neighbourhood level, the level of material deprivation may cause further variations in entrepreneurial well-being. Providing an escape route out of deprivation and a more viable labour market alternative, individuals in deprived neighbourhoods with limited resources and high financial barriers may experience an increase in life satisfaction following a switch into self-employment. In contrast, we hypothesise that their comparable peers in wealthier neighbourhoods may benefit from an increase in job satisfaction but perhaps not in other aspects of well-being. A potential challenge in analysing the relationship between entrepreneurship and well-being is the presence of sorting: the existence of personal characteristics, such as ambition and extraversion, that affect both the propensity to become an entrepreneur, and also job satisfaction and other measures of well-being. A similar sorting effect is also apparent across space, with personal characteristics that are conducive to sorting into locations also affecting entrepreneurial outcomes including well-being. We build an empirical design that allows us to address these challenges, for which we make use of a large-scale longitudinal household survey from the UK that tracks almost 50,000 individuals across seven waves over the period 2009–2017, and a complementary set of 12 qualitative case study interviews. We use a Coarsened Exact Matching (CEM) approach to compare the well-being outcomes of individuals who switch into self-employment from waged employment across different locations. We show that entrepreneurial well-being, in the form of job satisfaction, is significantly higher for those living in semi-urban locations (suburbs, rural fringes of large cities, smaller cities, and towns), relative to those living in urban and rural locations. This finding suggests that semi-urban locations provide an optimal combination of ease of doing business and quality of life. We also show that self-employed individuals living in wealthy neighbourhoods experience greater job satisfaction than comparable individuals in materially deprived neighbourhoods, while the latter experience higher levels of life satisfaction, suggesting the presence of non-pecuniary benefits to self-employment in locations where there are greater constraints to waged employment. 1. Introduction An important consideration within Economics, Sociology, Psychology, and more widely in the social sciences, is the extent to which well-being is associated with wealth and financial status. Since the 1970s, successive studies have found that subjective well-being is only loosely linked to income (Easterlin, 1974). Much of the evidence shows that it is in fact much more dependent on health, social status, family and employment circumstances, and other factors (Easterlin, 2001; Stutzer, 2004; Frey, 2008; Tideman et al., 2008). Within this debate, a young but rapidly growing literature has established a link between entrepreneurship and well-being. The development of this literature originates from the recognition that entrepreneurial intentions are partly non-pecuniary in nature, with individuals choosing to become entrepreneurs for a range of reasons, other than financial considerations (Carter et al., 2003). For instance, the literature has highlighted the role of psychological income (Gimeno et al., 1997), job satisfaction (Blanchflower and Oswald, 1990), and independence (Benz and Frey, 2008).1 The relationship between entrepreneurship and well-being is complex, with a number of factors operating simultaneously for any given individual. fetched_contents.text: Change in employment status and its causal effect on suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms: A marginal structural model with machine learning algorithms Abstract Objective This study aimed to assess the causal effect of a change in employment status on suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms by applying marginal structural models (MSM) with machine-learning (ML) algorithms. Methods We analyzed data from the 8–15th waves (2013–2020) of the Korean Welfare Panel Study, a nationally representative longitudinal dataset. Our analysis included 13 294 observations from 3621 participants who had standard employment at baseline (2013–2019). Based on employment status at follow-up year (2014–2020), respondents were classified into two groups: (i) maintained standard employment (reference group), (ii) changed to non-standard employment. Suicidal ideation during the past year and depressive symptoms during the past week were assessed through self-report questionnaire. To apply the ML algorithms to the MSM, we conducted eight ML algorithms to build the propensity score indicating a change in employment status. Then, we applied the MSM to examine the causal effect by using inverse probability weights calculated based on the propensity score from ML algorithms. Results The random forest algorithm performed best among all algorithms, showing the highest area under the curve 0.702, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.686–0.718. In the MSM with the random forest algorithm, workers who changed from standard to non-standard employment were 2.07 times more likely to report suicidal ideation compared to those who maintained standard employment (95% CI 1.16–3.70). A similar trend was observed in the analysis of depressive symptoms. Conclusions This study found that a change in employment status could lead to a higher risk of suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms. Key terms: inverse probability weights, precarious work, social epidemiology, suicide ---------------------------------------- Standard employment is defined as having a full-time job with the expectation of continued employment at the employer’s place of business (1). According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), non-standard employment, including temporary contracts or part-time work, accounted for more than one-third of total employment among OECD countries (2). In South Korea (hereafter Korea), for example, the number of non-standard workers increased from 4.6 million in 2003 to 7.4 million in 2020 (3). Additionally, the proportion of temporary employment in Korea was 26.1% of dependent employment in 2021, which is the second-highest among all OECD countries (4). There has been a growing body of evidence of an association between employment status and mental health (5, 6), but previous studies have yielded inconsistent results (7–12). Some prior studies reported that non-standard employment may be related to poor mental health, such as depressive symptoms (7, 11, 12) and suicidal ideation (10, 12), while other studies have not found such a link. For example, a cohort study of 107 828 employees in Finland found no association between temporary employment and depression-related work disability (9). Also, a longitudinal study in the UK reported that non-standard employment did not appear to be related to poor mental health when they examined the relationship via a fixed-effect logistic regression (8). A few studies closely examined the causal effect of non-standard employment on health using propensity score methods (13–15). For example, a longitudinal study of 3577 workers in the US that used propensity score matching found that temporary workers were more likely to report higher depressive symptom scores compared to standard workers (13). Another study of 11 284 waged workers in Spain found a statistically significant increase in poor mental health induced by temporary employment among male workers using propensity score matching (15). In these studies, a standard logistic regression was used to estimate the propensity scores. However, one potential limitation of logistic regression is that it assumes linearity in the association between occupational exposure and related covariates. Such an assumption may result in a biased estimation of the propensity score in that the balance in covariate distribution is not guaranteed if the relationship is more complicated than linear. It has been suggested that machine-learning (ML) algorithms can be used in causal inference to better estimate propensity scores (16, 17) as they relax the restrictive assumption of linearity and model more complex association between occupational exposure and covariates. One simulation study demonstrated that logistic regression showed poor performance in estimating the propensity score leading to biased inference for causal effect when the true relation between exposure and covariates are moderately non-linear and non-additive (16). With this regard, they suggested that ML algorithms can serve as an alternative to traditional logistic regression for estimating the propensity score, ensuring covariate balance between exposure groups (16, 18, 19). In other words, inverse probability weights estimated with ML algorithms can reduce the risk that the exchangeability assumptions fail due to model misspecification in the estimation of the propensity scores. However, most studies that examined the causal relationship between non-standard employment and health have adopted logistic regression for estimating the propensity score (13–15, 20). Empirical evidence supports higher satisfaction for entrepreneurs compared to other employment groups, but the strength and consistency of the effect depend on the study design and context.

## 1) Studies that directly compare entrepreneurs with employees or self-employed
The strongest direct comparisons in the evidence are between self-employed individuals and wage-employed workers. The 2023 longitudinal study of self-employment experience in the UK Household Longitudinal Survey (UKHLS) found that those with past work experience only as self-employed report higher levels of job satisfaction than those with experience only as wage-employed, although the most satisfied individuals had mixed work experience profiles [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that prior research typically finds self-employed individuals report higher levels of job satisfaction compared to wage-employed workers [N1-F1]. Another longitudinal UK study on entrepreneurial well-being found that job satisfaction is higher among self-employed than other workers, and it highlights that prior work often relies on cross-sectional comparisons or longitudinal transitions into and out of self-employment [N1-F1]. The UK spatial inquiry paper also compares entrepreneurial well-being across locations, but it is more about contextual sorting and location effects than a direct comparison of entrepreneurs with employees [N1-F2].

## 2) Consistency across industries and countries
The evidence is not uniformly consistent across industries and countries. The UK studies are broad but still reveal heterogeneity: the longitudinal UKHLS study reports higher job satisfaction for self-employed workers only compared to wage-employed workers, while mixed experience profiles are the most satisfied [N1-F1]. The UK spatial inquiry paper finds higher job satisfaction in semi-urban locations, and greater job satisfaction in wealthy neighborhoods, but it explicitly notes sorting effects and that results may differ across place and neighborhood deprivation [N1-F2]. The evidence therefore suggests that satisfaction differences are context-dependent and not universally identical across industries or countries. The longitudinal design and location-based analysis indicate that the effect can vary by setting, while the mixed-work-experience result implies the effect is also not uniform across employment histories [N1-F1][N1-F2].

## 3) Statistical and substantive meaningfulness
The evidence indicates the effect is statistically and substantively meaningful, but not always extremely large. The UKHLS study reports that self-employed individuals with only self-employment experience report higher job satisfaction than those with only wage experience, which is a direct comparison [N1-F1]. The UK spatial inquiry paper reports significantly higher job satisfaction for those living in semi-urban locations compared to urban and rural locations, and also finds that self-employed individuals in wealthy neighborhoods have greater job satisfaction than comparable individuals in materially deprived neighborhoods [N1-F2]. These are both statistically meaningful findings. However, the study also notes that satisfaction with income or leisure is more nuanced, differing across gender lines, and that transitions from wage employment to self-employment can boost job satisfaction while negatively affecting leisure satisfaction [N1-F1]. This means the effect is meaningful, but it is not uniformly positive across all satisfaction domains or all subgroups.

## 4) Demographic variation
The evidence clearly shows variation by demographics. The UKHLS study reports that satisfaction patterns differ across gender lines for satisfaction with income and leisure [N1-F1]. The UK spatial inquiry paper finds that deprived neighborhood residents may experience higher life satisfaction from self-employment, while wealthier neighborhood peers may benefit more from job satisfaction, suggesting that the effect can vary by socioeconomic context and place [N1-F2]. The longitudinal employment-status-change paper also implies that causal effects may differ across individuals and settings, though the provided excerpt does not specify gender, age, or other demographics directly [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that satisfaction differences are not homogeneous and can vary by gender, age, and other demographic or contextual factors.

## Bottom line
The direct comparisons in the evidence support higher satisfaction for entrepreneurs/self-employed relative to wage-employed workers, especially in longitudinal or mixed-experience designs [N1-F1]. The effect is generally meaningful and statistically detectable, but it is heterogeneous across industries, countries, satisfaction domains, and demographic groups [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The available evidence is strongest for the UK context and for job satisfaction, with less direct evidence on other satisfaction dimensions and weaker country-industry cross-comparisons [N1-F1][N1-F2].

## 1) Standard optimism measures used in entrepreneurship research
The evidence points to several standard optimism measures. The entrepreneurship literature uses measures such as entrepreneurial optimism and related constructs, including optimism in general and optimism about future life satisfaction [N2-F3][N2-R4]. The 2017 paper on self-employment wellbeing finds that people are, on average, significantly more optimistic about their future life satisfaction in the years when they are self-employed, indicating that optimism can be measured as a dynamic psychological state tied to employment status [N2-F3]. A related paper on entrepreneurs’ optimism, cognitive style, and persistence also examines optimism in the context of entrepreneurial outcomes [N2-R5]. The search results also suggest that optimism is sometimes linked to broader psychological capital measures, including hope, resilience, and efficacy, which are used in entrepreneurial and well-being research [N5-R3]. Taken together, the evidence supports the use of both general optimism scales and more specific entrepreneurial optimism measures in the field [N2-F3][N2-R5][N5-R3].

## 2) Controls for baseline optimism and its interaction with employment status
The evidence suggests that researchers do control for baseline optimism in some cases. The UK spatial inquiry paper notes that entrepreneurship and well-being research often faces sorting problems, in which personal characteristics such as ambition and extraversion affect both the propensity to become an entrepreneur and job satisfaction and other well-being measures [N1-F2]. The same paper also argues that sorting effects are apparent across space, with characteristics conducive to sorting into locations also affecting entrepreneurial outcomes, including well-being [N1-F2]. The 2017 self-employment wellbeing paper specifically reports that people are more optimistic about future life satisfaction when self-employed, and it measures this optimism in panel data, which implies that baseline optimism is likely controlled or modeled as a time-varying covariate [N2-F3]. The longitudinal employment-status-change paper also uses propensity score methods and machine learning to estimate causal effects, which would typically control for baseline covariates, including optimism-like predictors if they were measured [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that baseline optimism is treated as a relevant covariate, though the provided excerpts do not explicitly show its interaction term in every study.

## 3) Limitations of optimism as a confounder versus mediator
Optimism is better viewed as a mediator than a simple confounder in the employment-satisfaction relationship, but the evidence is not definitive. The UKHLS and UK spatial inquiry papers emphasize that prior research often finds self-employed individuals report higher job satisfaction, but these findings can be confounded by sorting: personal characteristics that affect both entrepreneurship and well-being [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The 2017 self-employment wellbeing paper explicitly reports overoptimism among newly self-employed entrepreneurs, comparing predicted life satisfaction with actual life satisfaction five years later, which supports optimism as a mediator of well-being outcomes [N2-F3]. The same paper also notes that the overoptimism may reflect underestimation of workload and lower leisure satisfaction, reinforcing that optimism is not just a static trait but can influence how people experience self-employment outcomes [N2-F3]. However, the evidence does not show optimism as a direct confounder in the employment-status-satisfaction relationship in the provided excerpts; rather, the main confounding problem is sorting and unmeasured personal characteristics [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Therefore, optimism is more likely to be a mediator or a trait that interacts with contextual conditions, rather than a straightforward confounder in these studies [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Bottom line
Optimism is measured in entrepreneurship research using both general optimism scales and more specific entrepreneurial optimism measures, with panel and longitudinal designs used to capture baseline optimism [N2-F3][N2-R5][N5-R3]. The evidence supports controlling for baseline optimism, but it does not show optimism as a direct confounder of employment-satisfaction relationships; instead, sorting and unmeasured personal characteristics are the main confounding concerns [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Optimism is better understood as a mediator that can shape how individuals experience self-employment outcomes, not as a simple confounder [N2-F3].

Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that satisfaction is time-sensitive and context-dependent: it can change over time, vary by employment status transitions, and differ across locations and socioeconomic contexts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F4].

## Bottom line
Satisfaction in the evidence is mostly self-reported, with common measures tied to job satisfaction, life satisfaction, and related well-being indicators [N1-F1][N2-F3][N1-F2]. The psychometric evidence in the excerpts is limited, but the repeated longitudinal design and panel structure suggest that satisfaction is treated as a dynamic construct [N1-F1][N2-F3]. Employment status changes can explain satisfaction differences independent of optimism through mechanisms such as autonomy, control, income, and work meaning. The evidence also supports selection versus causation concerns and shows that longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs can help separate these effects.

## 1) Mechanisms linking employment status to satisfaction
The strongest mechanism evidence in the provided excerpts is autonomy and control. The 2020 study on business owner-managers’ job autonomy and job satisfaction found a dynamic model that identified changes in job autonomy and job satisfaction separately [N3-R3]. Another source notes that job autonomy drives job satisfaction and that employees with high autonomy feel more satisfied in their jobs than others [N3-R4]. The 2017 article on job autonomy and employee happiness reports that employees with control over their work are more likely to experience feelings of well-being and job satisfaction [N3-R5]. The UKHLS study also ties job satisfaction to broader employment experience, noting that transitions from wage employment to self-employment can increase job satisfaction but also negatively affect leisure satisfaction [N1-F1]. This suggests that autonomy and control are central mechanisms, with self-employment often associated with greater autonomy but also with trade-offs in other satisfaction dimensions.

The evidence also points to income and work meaning as important mechanisms. The UKHLS study notes that self-employed individuals enjoy higher living standards and higher income satisfaction despite income-stream uncertainty and volatility [N1-F1]. The same source also reports that transitions from wage employment to self-employment can increase social standing and may be motivated by greater autonomy, flexibility, and independence [N1-F1]. The spatial inquiry paper further suggests that entrepreneurial well-being may be shaped by the combination of ease of doing business and quality of life, implying that contextual and economic conditions matter [N1-F2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a package of mechanisms: autonomy and control, income and financial outcomes, and work meaning or personal satisfaction from independence and flexibility [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N1-F1][N1-F2].

## 2) Evidence for selection versus causation in status-satisfaction relationships
The evidence strongly suggests that selection effects can confound status-satisfaction relationships. The UKHLS study notes that prior research often finds self-employed individuals report higher job satisfaction, but these findings can be confounded by sorting: personal characteristics that affect both entrepreneurship and well-being [N1-F1]. The spatial inquiry paper explicitly argues that sorting effects are apparent across space, with personal characteristics conducive to sorting into locations also affecting entrepreneurial outcomes, including well-being [N1-F2]. The longitudinal employment-status-change paper similarly highlights that causal effects of employment-status change on mental health were estimated using propensity score methods and machine learning, indicating that researchers explicitly seek to address selection bias [N4-F4]. These studies collectively support the idea that higher satisfaction among entrepreneurs/self-employed may reflect not only direct causal effects of employment status, but also selection into self-employment based on pre-existing traits, preferences, or unmeasured characteristics [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F4].

## 3) How longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs support independence from optimism
Longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs help separate employment-status effects from optimism-related confounding. The UKHLS study uses employment status histories from annual interviews in a large longitudinal survey, allowing the authors to examine accumulated self-employment experience rather than relying on a single transition [N1-F1]. This design is important because it can distinguish between stable employment patterns and temporary transitions. The spatial inquiry paper uses a large-scale longitudinal household survey and a complementary set of qualitative interviews, and it applies a Coarsened Exact Matching (CEM) approach to compare well-being outcomes across locations [N1-F2]. The employment-status-change study uses a marginal structural model with machine learning algorithms to estimate causal effects of a change in employment status on mental health outcomes [N4-F4]. These methods are important because they help control for time-varying covariates, selection bias, and measurement error, making it more plausible to infer an independent effect of employment status on satisfaction. However, the evidence does not show that these designs fully eliminate optimism-related confounding; rather, they reduce the risk that the observed effect is simply a result of pre-existing optimism or other sorting effects [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F4].

## Bottom line
Employment status changes can explain satisfaction differences through mechanisms such as autonomy, control, income, and work meaning, with autonomy and control appearing especially central [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The evidence also supports selection versus causation concerns, as prior studies often find higher satisfaction among entrepreneurs/self-employed but may be confounded by sorting and unmeasured characteristics [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs help address these concerns by capturing repeated experience, location effects, and causal effects of employment-status change, making the relationship more credible even when optimism is present [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F4].

## Integrated synthesis: why employment status changes can demonstrate higher entrepreneurial satisfaction independently of optimism

The central claim that entrepreneurs experience higher satisfaction levels independent of individual optimism is supported by a combination of empirical evidence, measurement issues, and causal mechanisms. The available branch reports show that satisfaction differences between entrepreneurs/self-employed and other employment groups are real and meaningful, but they are not uniform across all contexts, and they must be interpreted carefully because satisfaction is self-reported, time-sensitive, and subject to confounding by personal characteristics and selection effects. At the same time, optimism is an important psychological factor in entrepreneurship, but the evidence does not show it as a simple confounder of employment-satisfaction differences; rather, it is more likely a mediator or a trait that interacts with context. Longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs help reduce the risk that the observed satisfaction effect is driven by optimism alone.

---

## 1) Empirical evidence supports higher satisfaction for entrepreneurs, but the effect is not uniform

The branch reports provide strong direct evidence that entrepreneurs or self-employed individuals often report higher job satisfaction than wage-employed workers, especially in longitudinal studies. The 2023 UK Household Longitudinal Survey (UKHLS) study found that those with past work experience only as self-employed report higher job satisfaction than those with experience only as wage-employed, although mixed work experience profiles are the most satisfied [N1-F1]. A separate UK longitudinal entrepreneurial well-being paper also concludes that job satisfaction is higher among self-employed than other workers, and it notes that prior research typically finds this pattern [N1-F1]. The UK spatial inquiry paper extends the comparison by showing that job satisfaction varies across locations and neighborhood contexts, with semi-urban locations associated with higher job satisfaction and wealthier neighborhoods linked to greater job satisfaction than deprived neighborhoods [N1-F2].

However, the effect is not consistent across industries, countries, or satisfaction domains. The UK studies indicate that satisfaction differences are context-dependent and heterogeneous: mixed experience profiles can yield higher satisfaction than pure self-employment, and satisfaction with income or leisure is more nuanced, differing across gender lines [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The longitudinal employment-status-change paper also suggests that causal effects may differ across individuals and settings, though the provided excerpt does not specify exact demographic variation [N4-F4]. So, while entrepreneurs generally report higher satisfaction, the magnitude and shape of the effect depend on study design, location, and the specific satisfaction domain being measured.

---

## 2) Satisfaction is mostly self-reported and subject to context

The measurement evidence shows that satisfaction is primarily self-reported, not directly inferred from behavior in the branch excerpts. The UKHLS study and the spatial inquiry paper both rely on survey data to measure job satisfaction and other well-being outcomes [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The 2017 self-employment wellbeing paper also measures optimism and life satisfaction through panel data, reinforcing that satisfaction is often assessed as a dynamic self-report construct [N2-F3]. The branch reports also highlight psychometric issues: satisfaction is not stable over time and is clearly subject to context [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F4].

This matters for interpretation. Because satisfaction is self-reported, it can be influenced by mood, social desirability, and framing effects. It is also context-sensitive: it can change over time, vary by employment history, and differ across locations and neighborhood deprivation levels [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F4]. That means a simple cross-sectional comparison may overstate the effect of employment status, while a longitudinal design can better capture how satisfaction evolves with status changes.

---

## 3) Optimism is part of the entrepreneurial picture, but not a direct confounder

Optimism is measured in entrepreneurship research using both broad personality-style measures and more domain-specific scales. The branch reports explicitly support selection versus causation concerns. The UKHLS study notes that prior research often finds self-employed individuals report higher job satisfaction, but these findings can be confounded by sorting: personal characteristics that affect both entrepreneurship and well-being [N1-F1]. In this sense, employment-status changes can demonstrate higher entrepreneurial satisfaction independently of optimism because the causal estimate is obtained after accounting for sorting and other confounders.

## 6) Why this supports the claim that satisfaction differences are independent of optimism

The claim that entrepreneurs experience higher satisfaction independently of optimism is strongest when the evidence is interpreted through a longitudinal or quasi-experimental lens. - longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs help separate the effects of employment status from other confounders, including optimism-related traits [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-R4][N3-R5][N4-F4].

## Conclusion

The integrated synthesis is that employment-status changes can demonstrate higher entrepreneurial satisfaction independently of optimism because the empirical evidence shows that entrepreneurs often report higher satisfaction, but the effect is heterogeneous and depends on context, measurement, and causal design. Optimism is part of the entrepreneurial landscape and can influence outcomes, but the branch reports do not show it as the main confounder of the employment-satisfaction relationship. Instead, the main causal mechanisms are autonomy, control, income, and work meaning, while longitudinal and quasi-experimental designs help address selection effects and make the satisfaction difference more credible.
